content: An Emergency Medical Technician-Basic (EMT-B) is the foundational level of prehospital emergency medical care provider in the United States. EMT-Bs are employed across various industries and are not trained to deliver definitive medical care. Instead, their focus is on providing rapid, on-site treatment and transporting patients to higher-level medical providers. EMT-Bs collaborate with other medical professionals, including paramedics, nurses, physicians, and fellow EMT-Bs. Their actions in the prehospital setting are guided by protocols and procedures established by the physician medical director of their system. Education and Training The training for EMT-Bs is regulated at both state and federal levels. At the federal level, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) has established a minimum curriculum, known as the National Standard Curriculum, which all states must meet. This curriculum includes 110 hours of lecture and laboratory instruction covering topics such as anatomy, physiology, legal aspects of medical care, and the assessment and treatment of medical, trauma, behavioral, and obstetric emergencies. In addition to classroom instruction, the NHTSA recommends clinical rotations in ambulances and emergency departments. However, these experiences are less standardized due to local variations. The National Registry of Emergency Medical Technicians (NREMT) has developed certification exams for the NHTSA EMT levels, including EMT-Basic. As of 2006, 39 U.S. states use the NREMT EMT-Basic exam as part of their licensing or certification process. Once certified, EMT-Basics must complete continuing education hours to recertify at the end of their certification period. Recertification requirements vary by state. Continuing education courses may include topics relevant to EMT-Basic work, ranging from foundational subjects like anatomy, physiology, or psychology to applied courses such as Prehospital Trauma Life Support (PHTLS). These courses may be standardized or tailored to the needs of specific EMS systems or regions. Scope of Practice The scope of practice for EMT-Bs is regulated by state law and can vary significantly between states and even within states. Generally, EMT-Bs provide basic life support and are limited to non-invasive procedures. Their skills include basic medical assessment, cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), automated external defibrillation (AED), mechanical ventilation using a bag-valve mask, placement of airway adjuncts such as oropharyngeal and nasopharyngeal airways, splinting (including spinal immobilization and traction splints), and suctioning. EMT-Bs are also trained to assist patients with the administration of prescribed medications, such as nitroglycerin, metered-dose inhalers (e.g., albuterol), and epinephrine auto-injectors (e.g., EpiPen). Each state has the authority to modify the scope of practice for EMT-Bs. For example, EMT-Bs in California (referred to as EMT-Is) are not permitted to administer activated charcoal under standard certification. However, counties in California can apply to the state to expand the scope of practice for EMT-Basics to include interventions like activated charcoal and other pharmaceutical treatments not typically allowed. In contrast, Oregon permits EMT-Bs to use advanced airway devices, such as the pharyngeal esophageal airway device. An example of such a device is the Combitube.
